records.medicinalUses: Clinical evidence supports antifungal and antiscabies activity, including topical use for ringworm and other fungal skin infections.
records.preparationMethod: Grind enough fresh Akapulko leaves to obtain extract and apply it to the affected skin. Recorded guidance also describes a cooled leaf decoction as an alternative wash if the fresh extract causes allergy.
records.dosage: Apply the extract or cooled wash to the affected area twice daily for up to 3 weeks, following the recorded guidance.
records.warnings: For external use. Stop use if an allergic or severe skin reaction occurs, and seek professional advice if the condition persists, spreads, or is uncertain.

sources.title: PITAHC Directory of Herbs

records.medicinalUses: Clinical evidence has evaluated Ampalaya for blood-sugar control and metabolic syndrome. Its use should remain under professional guidance.
records.preparationMethod: Under health-professional guidance, eating Ampalaya leaves as salad or with meals, or boiling 2 cups of sprouts in 2 glasses of water until half remains, then straining the decoction.
records.dosage: Recorded guidance describes 1 cup of leaves twice daily, or ⅓ of the prepared decoction 3 times daily, 30 minutes before meals, when advised by a health professional.
records.warnings: Diabetes requires diagnosis and monitoring by a health professional. Do not replace or change prescribed diabetes treatment without medical advice.

sources.title: PITAHC Directory of Herbs

records.medicinalUses: Philippine research records traditional leaf use for abdominal pain, diarrhea, boils, fatigue, fever, and inflammation, alongside laboratory antiparasitic, insecticidal, and anticancer findings. None of these laboratory findings establishes a cancer treatment.
records.preparationMethod: Traditional oral preparation withheld: TRAMIL reports a Caribbean Annona reticulata leaf decoction but warns about neurotoxicity associated with prolonged consumption. Its English recipe also contains inconsistent salt units. This does not establish a safe Philippine home recipe. Boiling instructions and treatment quantities are not imported.
records.dosage: No verified human treatment dose is supplied.
records.warnings: Do not use Anonas leaf preparations to replace treatment for infection, fever, parasites or cancer. TRAMIL warns about neurotoxicity associated with prolonged consumption and excludes medicinal use during pregnancy, breastfeeding and in children under twelve. A safe home treatment dose is not established here.

records.dosage: No verified human treatment dose is supplied.
records.warnings: No validated preparation or dose is provided. Diarrhea with dehydration, blood, fever, or persistent symptoms requires medical care.

records.preparationMethod: Documented traditional preparation: the Ayta study reports leaves and shoots applied externally to the forehead for fever. No processing sequence or duration is specified. This is a report, not validated fever treatment; seed food colouring uses a different part.
records.dosage: No verified human treatment dose is supplied.
records.warnings: The leaves are not interchangeable with culinary seed coloring. No safe medicinal preparation or dose is established; burns and infected wounds require proper care.

records.medicinalUses: Clinical studies have evaluated garlic for hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and arteriosclerosis.
records.preparationMethod: Consult a health center for diagnosis and advice. Recorded guidance notes that a health professional may advise garlic soaked in vinegar, sterilized, grilled, or fried in a little oil and taken with meals.
records.dosage: Recorded guidance states that a health professional may advise 2–3 garlic bulbs, 3 times daily with breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
records.warnings: Reported side effects include vomiting, heartburn, diarrhea, allergies, contact dermatitis, or asthma. Dog and snake bites require immediate wound washing and urgent medical care, not garlic treatment.

records.medicinalUses: Clinical evidence includes gingivitis and acute diarrhea. Traditional use includes a topical wash for wounds or scabies and a gargle for swollen gums.
records.preparationMethod: For wounds or scabies, boil 1–2 handfuls of leafy tops in a small pot of water, cool to lukewarm, and use as a wash. For swollen gums, boil 1 handful, cool, and use as a gargle.
records.dosage: Recorded guidance describes using the lukewarm wash or gargle twice daily while symptoms improve.
records.warnings: Consult a health professional if symptoms persist or if fever, spreading redness, or other signs of infection occur. Never apply hot liquid to skin or gums.

records.preparationMethod: Documented traditional preparation: the Ayta study records oral leaf decoction or sap for respiratory complaints. Amounts, water volume and duration are not specified. This is Artemisia vulgaris, not Artemisia absinthium; the report does not establish a safe treatment recipe.
records.dosage: No verified human treatment dose is supplied.
records.warnings: No clinically validated preparation or dose is provided. Avoid medicinal use during pregnancy unless specifically cleared by a qualified clinician; persistent cough or diarrhea needs assessment.

records.preparationMethod: Food preparation only: NParks describes Colocasia esculenta leaves and petioles cooked as vegetables and warns against eating raw material because of calcium oxalate. No leaf cooking time or medicinal dose is supplied. This is not a preparation for hypertension or itching; the source distinguishes this species from look-alike aroids.
records.dosage: No verified human treatment dose is supplied.
records.warnings: Raw or improperly prepared gabi can irritate the mouth and skin. Food preparation is not a medicinal dose, and prescribed blood-pressure treatment should not be replaced.

records.medicinalUses: A Philippine pilot study in 12 patients found that a standardized 4% Hibiscus rosa-sinensis leaf-extract ointment, used alongside compression stockings, showed potential for venous leg ulcer closure. This small adjunct study does not establish effectiveness for general wound treatment.
records.preparationMethod: The human study used a standardized 4% leaf-extract ointment together with medical compression therapy. It does not provide a safe home-preparation method.
records.dosage: Research protocol only: the standardized ointment was applied twice daily for up to 12 weeks under dermatology care. This is not a self-treatment dosage.
records.warnings: Open or chronic wounds require professional assessment. Do not place homemade plant extracts on ulcers, infected wounds, or broken skin, and do not replace compression or prescribed wound care.

records.medicinalUses: Reviews document traditional uses and laboratory or animal findings for Heliotropium indicum, but human clinical studies are still needed to establish effectiveness and a safe therapeutic dose.

records.preparationMethod: The study records decoctions or alcohol-based preparations of bark, branches and roots. This describes reported traditional practice only; it is not a home-preparation instruction.
records.dosage: No clinically validated human dosage is established by the cited ethnobotanical study. Reported community quantities must not be treated as safe or effective doses.
records.warnings: Traditional-use reports do not establish clinical safety. A separate leaf-extract toxicity study was conducted in mice, not people; it cannot establish human safety, a safe dose or suitability in pregnancy or childhood. Educational record only; seek qualified medical advice rather than self-treating.

Its all-ages frequency claim is not adopted as safe dosing; sterility and safe application duration are not established.
records.dosage: No verified human treatment dose is supplied.
records.warnings: Do not use the plant for snakebite, suspected malaria, fracture, or serious infection. No safe internal preparation or dose is established.

records.preparationMethod: Boil crushed fresh Lagundi leaves in 2 cups of water until only half of the water remains. Keep the pot uncovered once it starts boiling.
records.dosage: Amount of crushed leaves recorded in the source guidance: 1½ tablespoons for ages 2–6, 3 tablespoons for ages 7–12, and 6 tablespoons for ages 13 and above.
records.warnings: Consult a health professional for diagnosis and advice, especially for young children or if a cough persists or worsens.

records.dosage: No verified human treatment dose is supplied.

records.preparationMethod: The cited research used measured oral ginger preparations, not a standardized home tea recipe.
records.dosage: No home-treatment dose is provided. Discuss pregnancy-related nausea and any supplement with a qualified clinician.
records.warnings: Ginger can cause heartburn, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, or mouth and throat irritation. Check for medicine interactions; breastfeeding safety information is limited.

records.preparationMethod: Research used a specific extract in capsules. Kitchen turmeric, isolated curcumin, and enhanced-absorption supplements are not interchangeable.
records.dosage: No home-treatment dose is provided; product composition and clinical suitability require professional review.
records.warnings: Turmeric supplements can cause digestive upset. Liver injury has been reported with some enhanced-absorption curcumin products. Stop use and seek care for jaundice or dark urine. Supplement use in pregnancy may be unsafe.

records.preparationMethod: Traditional oral preparation withheld: human case reports linked identified Tinospora crispa ingestion to toxic hepatitis, including aqueous extracts of fresh stems, not only powdered products. records.dosage: No verified human treatment dose is supplied.

Supplements do not replace breastfeeding assessment and support.
records.preparationMethod: The cited trial used leaf capsules. Cooked leaves and differently formulated supplements should not be treated as equivalent research preparations.
records.dosage: No general lactation dose is supplied. A health professional should assess feeding difficulties and the suitability of any supplement.
records.warnings: Long-term benefits and risks for breastfed infants remain insufficiently studied. Use caution with supplements if at risk of blood clots; discuss use with a clinician.

records.warnings: Do not exceed the listed seed count. Overconsumption may cause nausea, hiccups, stomach pain, or diarrhea. Consult a health professional for diagnosis and treatment of suspected intestinal worms.

records.dosage: No verified human treatment dose is supplied.

records.medicinalUses: A small acne trial found greater improvement with a prepared aloe gel plus tretinoin than tretinoin with its comparison gel. This supports further study of the combination, not a claim that raw aloe alone treats acne or all wounds.
records.preparationMethod: The study used a formulated topical gel alongside prescription treatment. Inner gel, yellow latex, and whole-leaf extracts have different safety profiles; no home extraction method is supplied.
records.dosage: No homemade or oral medicinal dose is supplied. Do not copy study formulations into a personal treatment plan.
records.warnings: Topical aloe can cause irritation or rash. Oral latex may cause cramps and diarrhea; oral leaf extracts have been linked to hepatitis. Oral use may be unsafe during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Do not infer oral safety from topical studies.
